title: Operators
description: Python's arithmetic, comparison, logical, bitwise, membership, and identity operators, plus precedence.
objectives: Use arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators correctly

content.heading: Operator Categories
content.body:
Arithmetic operators are + - * / (true division, always returns a float) // (floor division) % (modulus) and ** (exponentiation). Comparison operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) return booleans and can be chained: 1 < x < 10 is valid Python and means (1 < x) and (x < 10). Logical operators are the words and, or, and not (not symbols like && in C/Java); they short-circuit, meaning the second operand is only evaluated if needed. Assignment operators include the augmented forms (+=, -=, *=, /=, //=, %=, **=), which modify a variable's binding in place syntactically (though for immutable types this still creates a new object).

Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) work on the binary representation of integers. Membership operators, in and not in, test whether a value exists inside a sequence or collection (e.g., 3 in [1,2,3]). Identity operators, is and is not, test whether two names refer to the exact same object — not whether their values are equal.

content.heading: Precedence and Associativity
content.body: Python evaluates expressions according to a well-defined precedence order (highest to lowest, roughly): parentheses, exponentiation (**), unary +/-, multiplication/division/floor-division/modulus, addition/subtraction, bitwise shifts, bitwise AND, bitwise XOR, bitwise OR, comparisons, not, and, or. When operators share precedence, most are left-associative (evaluated left to right), except ** which is right-associative (2 ** 3 ** 2 is 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 512). When in doubt, use parentheses to make evaluation order explicit — this avoids subtle bugs and makes code more readable.

content.code:
print(7 // 2, 7 % 2, 2 ** 10)   # 3 1 1024
print(1 < 5 < 10)               # True (chained comparison)
print(3 in [1, 2, 3])           # True

a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b, a is b)           # True False — equal value, different objects
content.explanation: a == b compares values (both lists contain 1, 2, so True); a is b compares identity — they are two separate list objects in memory, so False.

keyPoints: / always produces a float; // performs floor division
and/or/not are the logical operators, written as words
== checks value equality; is checks object identity
** is right-associative; most other operators are left-associative
commonMistakes: Using is to compare values instead of == (works by accident for small cached ints, fails for most other objects)
Forgetting / always returns a float even for two integers
Misjudging precedence and omitting parentheses in a complex expression
